r1004.passage: In her memoir, chef Rosa Delgado recalls that her grandmother's recipes were less instructions than : "a pinch of this," "enough" of that, and a reminder to taste and adjust. They assumed the cook already knew what the finished dish should taste like.
choices: prescriptions
inventories
transcriptions
suggestions
r1004.explain: "Less instructions than " needs something looser than instructions, and the examples ("a pinch," "enough," "taste and adjust") are vague guidance. Suggestions fits. Prescriptions would be even more exact than instructions, and inventories (lists of ingredients) misses the guidance about method.

r1005.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
r1005.passage: Economist Ama Owusu argues that the cash-transfer program's benefits were real but . Payments reached nearly every eligible household in the first year, yet within three years most families' incomes had fallen back to where they were before the program began.
choices: short-lived
pervasive
superficial
negligible
r1005.explain: The evidence is about time: benefits were felt widely at first but faded within three years. Short-lived captures that. Trap: pervasive matches the first year only. Negligible contradicts "real," and superficial (shallow) isn't what the time-based evidence shows.

r1006.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
r1006.passage: Some readers regard the unresolved ending of Mira Castellanos's novel as , but Castellanos insists that leaving the central mystery unsolved was intentional: in her view, a tidy resolution would have betrayed the uncertainty her characters live with.
choices: an homage
a revelation
a compromise
an oversight
r1006.explain: "But Castellanos insists that leaving the mystery unsolved was intentional" answers a charge that it was unintentional, so readers see it as an oversight. A compromise implies a deliberate trade-off, which is closer to the author's view than to her critics'.

r1007.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
r1007.passage: Architect Jun Park's design for the new public library is strikingly . Rather than ordering new materials, it reuses the brick, the timber beams, and even the steel window frames of the shoe factory that once stood on the site.
choices: ostentatious
resourceful
derivative
provisional
r1007.explain: The design makes clever use of what was already there, which is resourceful. Trap: derivative means imitating someone else's work; reusing a building's materials isn't copying a design. Ostentatious (showy) clashes with the thrift described.

r1008.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
r1008.passage: Linguist Omar Haddad notes that the coastal dialect's vocabulary is remarkably : words borrowed from Arabic, Portuguese, Hindi, and Swahili sit side by side, and speakers often draw on three or four of these sources in a single sentence.
choices: archaic
insular
eclectic
esoteric
r1008.explain: Words drawn from many sources, used together, make the vocabulary eclectic. Insular (closed off from outside influence) is the opposite. Nothing says the words are old (archaic) or understood only by specialists (esoteric).

r1009.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
r1009.passage: Early reviewers dismissed the painter's interest in industrial scenes as a passing , but she returned to factories, cranes, and rail yards again and again over the next four decades.
choices: obsession
conviction
commission
whim
r1009.explain: The reviewers expected the interest to be brief ("passing") and unserious ("dismissed"): a whim. The "but" clause shows they were wrong. Trap: obsession describes what the interest turned out to be, and "a passing obsession" contradicts itself.

r1010.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
r1010.passage: The senator's statement on the trade agreement was carefully : she praised its labor protections and criticized its environmental provisions but declined to say how she would vote.
choices: conciliatory
unequivocal
noncommittal
dismissive
r1010.explain: Praise for one part, criticism of another, and no stated vote: she avoided taking a position, so the statement was noncommittal. Unequivocal means the opposite. Trap: conciliatory (meant to make peace) captures the mixed tone but not the refusal to commit.

r1011.sub: Uncommon sense of a common word
r1011.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
r1011.passage: The park ranger's praise for the Copper Ridge trail was : she called it the most beautiful route in the park but warned that its loose rock made it unsuitable for anyone without climbing experience.
choices: unreserved
qualified
grudging
effusive
r1011.explain: Here qualified means limited by a condition: the praise comes with a serious warning attached. Unreserved and effusive describe praise without limits. Trap: grudging means given reluctantly, but the ranger isn't reluctant; she calls it the most beautiful route.

r1012.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
r1012.passage: In his wartime letters home, the general's confident tone occasionally his private doubts: a reassurance repeated a little too often, a plan described in suspiciously exhaustive detail.
choices: betrays
conceals
resolves
exaggerates
r1012.explain: The examples after the colon are clues that leak through the confident surface, so the tone sometimes betrays (unintentionally reveals) his doubts. Trap: a confident tone usually conceals doubt, but the colon lists signs of doubt showing through, the opposite of concealment.

r1013.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
r1013.passage: Sociologist Imani Clarke cautions that the importance of rural libraries is easily by circulation statistics, which count the books residents borrow but not the hours they spend using library computers, attending classes, or getting help with tax forms.
choices: inflated
understated
documented
replaced
r1013.explain: Circulation figures miss much of what libraries do, so they make libraries look less important than they are: the importance is understated. Trap: inflated reverses the direction of the error.

r1014.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
r1014.passage: The new observations do not overturn the theory of planet formation so much as it: the theory's central claim survives, but its predictions now appear to hold only for stars within a narrower range of masses than astronomers had assumed.
choices: circumscribe
corroborate
supplant
popularize
r1014.explain: The theory survives but now applies to fewer stars: its scope is limited, or circumscribed. Supplant means replace, which "do not overturn" rules out. Trap: corroborate (confirm) fits "survives" but ignores the narrowing.

r1015.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
r1015.passage: Unlike her contemporaries, who filled their canvases with crowded markets and elaborate interiors, the painter favored compositions: a single tree, a strip of horizon, and broad fields of unbroken color.
choices: ornate
vivid
cluttered
spare
r1015.explain: A single tree, a strip of horizon, and unbroken color describe minimal compositions, which are spare, in contrast to her contemporaries' crowded scenes. Ornate and cluttered describe the contemporaries. Vivid (bright) isn't supported.

r1016.sub: A suspicion that turns out wrong
r1016.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
r1016.passage: Marine chemist Leilani Kahale initially suspected that her temperature readings had been by a faulty sensor. But recalibrating the instrument changed none of the readings, and she concluded that the unusually warm water was real.
choices: confirmed
supplemented
distorted
anticipated
r1016.explain: She suspected the sensor had made the readings inaccurate (distorted) and then found it hadn't, so the warm water was real. Trap: confirmed is what she eventually concluded about the water, not what she suspected the sensor did.

r1017.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
r1017.passage: The playwright's dialogue is deceptively . Her characters speak in short, ordinary sentences, yet nearly every line carries a second meaning that becomes clear only when the play is seen a second time.
choices: ornate
opaque
verbose
simple
r1017.explain: "Deceptively" means appearing one way while being another. The dialogue looks plain (short, ordinary sentences) but holds hidden meanings, so it is deceptively simple. Ornate and verbose contradict "short, ordinary sentences." Trap: opaque describes the hidden meanings, but "deceptively opaque" would mean the dialogue only seems hard to understand.

r1018.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
r1018.passage: Historians once regarded the mountain trade route as to the region's economy, a minor path used by a handful of traveling merchants. Newly translated tax records, however, show that it carried more goods than any other route in the region.
choices: peripheral
integral
detrimental
antecedent
r1018.explain: The old view is glossed right after the blank: "a minor path." That is peripheral, of little importance. Trap: integral is what the new records show, the view the "however" sentence contrasts with.

r1019.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
r1019.passage: Because the vaccine must stay frozen until shortly before use, its distribution in remote areas has been : clinics without reliable freezers have received far fewer doses than urban hospitals.
choices: accelerated
uneven
uniform
unprecedented
r1019.explain: Some places get far fewer doses than others, so distribution is uneven. Uniform is the opposite, and nothing indicates speed or novelty.

r1020.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
r1020.passage: Physicist Dara Okonkwo describes her lab's new particle detector as rather than revolutionary: it uses the same basic design as earlier instruments, but nearly every component has been refined to reduce background noise.
choices: derivative
experimental
incremental
obsolete
r1020.explain: Same design, many small refinements: progress by steps, which is incremental. Trap: derivative suggests unoriginal copying, a criticism; the text describes improvement, and Okonkwo is describing her own lab's work favorably.

r1021.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
r1021.passage: In her essay, Noor Siddiqui's tone toward her childhood town is : she writes fondly of its harvest festivals and its neighbors' kindness, yet she also recounts, without softening it, the narrowness of outlook that eventually drove her to leave.
choices: ambivalent
nostalgic
scathing
indifferent
r1021.explain: Fondness and criticism together make the tone ambivalent (mixed). Nostalgic covers only the fond half and scathing only the critical half. Indifferent (not caring) contradicts both.

r1022.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
r1022.passage: Anthropologist Kenji Mori found that the island's fishing rules, though never written down, were observed: during two years of fieldwork, he recorded only three violations.
choices: sporadically
nominally
scrupulously
reluctantly
r1022.explain: Only three violations in two years means the rules were followed carefully, or scrupulously. Sporadically (occasionally) and nominally (in name only) reverse the evidence. Nothing indicates reluctance.

r1023.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
r1023.passage: Although the museum's founders intended its collection to be , acquiring objects from every continent and historical period, budget shortfalls meant that by 1950 the collection consisted mostly of pottery from nearby towns.
choices: provincial
encyclopedic
esoteric
ephemeral
r1023.explain: The founders' intention is glossed after the comma: objects from everywhere and every period. That is encyclopedic. Trap: provincial describes what the collection actually became, the outcome the "although" sentence contrasts with the intention.

r1024.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
r1024.passage: Ecologists introduced barn owls to the island in hopes that the birds would the growth of its rat population. Instead, the owls preyed mostly on native seabirds, and the number of rats kept climbing.
choices: mirror
document
accelerate
check
r1024.explain: The ecologists hoped the owls would hold back the rats; here check means restrain. "Instead … the number of rats kept climbing" shows the hope failed. Accelerate reverses the goal; mirror and document aren't things predators do to prey.

r1025.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
r1025.passage: The newly digitized census data the long-standing assumption that the town's population peaked in 1920: the figures show that it continued to grow for another two decades.
choices: reinforce
explain
predate
undercut
r1025.explain: Data showing growth after 1920 contradict the assumption of a 1920 peak, so they undercut it. Reinforce is the reverse.

r1026.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
r1026.passage: The diplomat was known for her : in negotiations, she rarely revealed her own position until the other side had fully stated theirs, and she seldom spoke to the press at all.
choices: reticence
candor
volatility
magnanimity
r1026.explain: Withholding her position and avoiding the press show reticence, a reluctance to reveal thoughts. Candor (frankness) is the opposite. Nothing suggests mood swings (volatility) or generosity (magnanimity).

r1027.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
r1027.passage: Rather than the earlier study's findings, as some critics had expected, the new paper accepts them and builds on them, returning to the same field sites to ask a question the original authors never considered.
choices: extending
citing
challenging
applying
r1027.explain: "Rather than … the new paper accepts them" sets up a contrast with accepting, so the blank must mean rejecting or disputing: challenging. Trap: extending describes what the paper actually does.

r1028.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
r1028.passage: The poet's late work is often called , but her notebooks suggest that its compressed, fragmentary lines were not a sign of declining powers but a deliberate experiment with silence and omission.
choices: experimental
faltering
prolific
derivative
r1028.explain: The notebooks rebut a charge of "declining powers," so critics call the work faltering. Trap: experimental is the poet's own view, which the notebooks support, not the critics' label.

r1029.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
r1029.passage: Pharmacologist Sunita Rao warns that the drug's benefits, though statistically significant, are : patients who took it recovered, on average, only half a day sooner than those who received a placebo.
choices: spurious
substantial
modest
inconsistent
r1029.explain: The colon shows the benefit is small: half a day. Modest fits. Substantial reverses it. Trap: spurious (false) contradicts "statistically significant": the benefit is real, just small.

r1030.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
r1030.passage: Medieval European world maps were not representations of geography. Many placed Jerusalem at the center and illustrated scenes from scripture, reflecting the mapmakers' beliefs as much as the shape of the land.
choices: symbolic
literal
decorative
ambitious
r1030.explain: The maps reflected beliefs as much as geography, so they were not straightforward, literal depictions. Trap: symbolic describes what the maps were, so "not symbolic" contradicts the evidence. The illustrations make decorative tempting, but "not decorative" is also contradicted.

r2001.sub: Main idea of a literary passage
r2001.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
r2001.passage:
The following text is from a novel. Teodora has just been promoted to head chef of the restaurant where she has worked for nine years.

Teodora had imagined the moment many times, and in every version she felt triumphant. Instead, standing in the empty kitchen after the others had gone home, she noticed only the small things she would now be responsible for: the hum of the walk-in freezer, the knife with the loose handle, the schedule taped crookedly to the wall. The promotion had not lifted a weight from her; it had handed her a new one, and she was surprised to find that she did not mind its heft.
choices: Teodora's promotion brings responsibilities she hadn't expected, and she finds she is willing to carry them.
Teodora regrets accepting a promotion that she now realizes will keep her in the kitchen long after the others leave.
Teodora feels just as triumphant about her promotion as she had always imagined she would.
Teodora worries that the restaurant's equipment, including the freezer and the knives, is in poor condition.
r2001.explain: Her imagined triumph gives way to a sense of new responsibility ("handed her a new one"), but she "did not mind its heft." B ignores that final acceptance; C contradicts "Instead." The freezer and the loose knife are examples of responsibility, not the main point (D).

r2002.sub: Main idea of a dense informational text
r2002.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
r2002.passage: Researchers once believed that trees in a forest compete with one another for every resource. Studies by forest ecologist Mei Takahashi suggest a more complicated picture. Underground networks of fungi connect the roots of many trees, and through them, carbon and nutrients can pass from one tree to another. In Takahashi's experiments, seedlings shaded by taller trees received carbon through these networks, which helped them survive until a gap opened in the canopy above.
choices: Fungi that connect the roots of different trees harm the trees by drawing carbon and nutrients from them.
Seedlings shaded by taller trees grow faster than seedlings that receive direct sunlight.
Research suggests that trees can share resources through fungal networks, not only compete for them.
Forest ecologists now agree that trees in a forest never compete with one another for resources.
r2002.explain: The text revises the old view of pure competition by describing resource sharing through fungal networks. D overstates the revision: "more complicated" isn't "never compete." B misreads the seedling detail; the carbon helped them survive, not grow faster than seedlings in the sun.

r2003.sub: A detail about a character's motive
r2003.stem: According to the text, why does Mr. Ferris begin to involve the boy's mother in the lessons?
r2003.passage:
The following text is from a short story. Mr. Ferris, a retired schoolteacher, has started tutoring his neighbor's son.

The boy was quick, quicker than he let on, and Mr. Ferris soon understood that the wrong answers were not mistakes. Each time the boy erred, his mother, listening from the next room, would come in to sit beside him. Mr. Ferris began, without saying anything, to leave the door open and to pause, now and then, to ask the mother what she thought.
choices: He believes that the mother understands the subject better than he does and can explain it more clearly.
He realizes that the boy gives wrong answers on purpose so that his mother will join him.
He wants the mother to see for herself how poorly her son is doing in his lessons.
He finds that the boy's questions are often too difficult for him to answer without help.
r2003.explain: Mr. Ferris sees that "the wrong answers were not mistakes": each error brings the mother into the room. Leaving the door open and asking her opinion gives the boy the company he was seeking. C assumes the boy is struggling, which the text contradicts ("quick, quicker than he let on").

r2004.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
r2004.passage: Lab-grown diamonds are chemically identical to mined diamonds and can now be produced for a fraction of the cost. Jewelers once predicted that consumers would never accept them, but sales have risen steadily, especially among younger buyers. Economist Rosa Lind argues that this shift may permanently lower the prices of mined diamonds, whose value has depended largely on the belief that they are rare.
choices: Lab-grown diamonds are chemically different from mined diamonds and are therefore less valuable to most buyers.
Younger consumers prefer mined diamonds to lab-grown diamonds because they believe mined diamonds are rare.
Jewelers have successfully persuaded consumers to reject lab-grown diamonds despite their lower cost.
Wider acceptance of lab-grown diamonds may lower the value of mined diamonds, which depends on scarcity.
r2004.explain: The text describes rising acceptance of lab-grown diamonds and Lind's argument about its effect on mined-diamond prices. A contradicts "chemically identical." B and C reverse the sales trend.

r2005.stem: Which choice best describes how the speaker's father communicates with her, according to the text?
r2005.passage:
The following text is from a poem. The speaker describes her father's workshop.

Every tool had a painted outline on the pegboard,
so you could see at a glance what was missing.
He never told me to put things back.
He only stood, some evenings, looking at the wall,
at the white shape of a saw I had borrowed,
until I brought it home.
choices: He scolds her whenever she forgets to return one of his tools to its place on the pegboard.
He refuses to let her borrow his tools until she promises to put each one back.
He writes notes on the pegboard beside each outline reminding her what she needs to return.
He conveys his expectations silently, through the outlines and his attention to them.
r2005.explain: "He never told me to put things back"; instead he stood looking at the empty outline until she returned the saw. He communicates without words. A contradicts "never told me." She had borrowed the saw, so B is wrong too.

r2006.sub: Main idea of a historical account
r2006.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
r2006.passage: In the 1850s, London's River Thames carried the city's untreated sewage, and during the hot summer of 1858 the smell became so overwhelming that Parliament, which met beside the river, considered relocating. The crisis, known as the Great Stink, finally pushed lawmakers to fund engineer Joseph Bazalgette's plan for a vast network of sewers that carried waste away from the city center. Completed over the following decades, the system sharply reduced outbreaks of cholera, though most officials at the time still believed the disease spread through foul air rather than contaminated water.
choices: Parliament moved away from the Thames after the Great Stink of 1858 made its meeting place unbearable.
A stench in 1858 led to sewers that improved public health, though officials misunderstood cholera.
Joseph Bazalgette's sewer system proved to officials that cholera was spread through contaminated water.
London's sewers were completed within a single year after the Great Stink, ending cholera outbreaks.
r2006.explain: The text links the Great Stink to funding for the sewers, notes the drop in cholera, and adds that officials held the wrong theory of disease. A confuses "considered relocating" with relocating. C isn't stated, and D contradicts "over the following decades."

r2007.sub: A character's perspective on a change
r2007.stem: Which choice best describes Abuela Carmen's attitude toward the change described in the text?
r2007.passage:
The following text is from a novel. Abuela Carmen has lived in the same apartment for fifty years.

When the building's new owners replaced the old iron mailboxes with gleaming steel ones, the other tenants were delighted. Abuela Carmen said nothing, but every morning she went down to check her new box at exactly the time the mail had always come, though the carrier now arrived in the afternoon. "The box is new," she told her grandson. "I am not."
choices: She keeps to her long-standing habits even though her surroundings have changed.
She is privately as delighted by the new mailboxes as the other tenants are but keeps it to herself.
She resents the new owners for replacing the mailboxes and refuses to use her new box.
She is confused about when the mail now arrives because the carrier's schedule has changed.
r2007.explain: She keeps checking at the old time, and her line "The box is new. I am not" shows she knowingly holds to her routine. The text says she "said nothing," so C fails. D misreads deliberate habit as confusion.

r2008.sub: Main idea with a surprising result
r2008.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
r2008.passage: When a city in the Netherlands removed traffic lights, signs, and curbs from a busy intersection, planners expected chaos. Instead, accidents fell. Traffic engineer Hans Monderman, who designed the change, argued that drivers who are unsure who has the right of way slow down and make eye contact with pedestrians and cyclists, while clear rules invite drivers to stop paying attention. Critics note, however, that the approach may be harder for people with visual impairments, who rely on curbs and signals to navigate.
choices: Traffic lights and signs are the main cause of accidents at busy intersections in Dutch cities.
Drivers in the Netherlands pay closer attention to pedestrians and cyclists than drivers in other countries do.
Removing traffic controls from one intersection reduced accidents, though the approach has drawbacks.
Pedestrians with visual impairments prefer intersections without curbs because they are easier to cross.
r2008.explain: The text reports the surprising drop in accidents, Monderman's explanation, and the critics' concern. A overgeneralizes from one intersection; D reverses the critics' point.

r2009.sub: Main idea of a two-part claim
r2009.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
r2009.passage: Octopuses can change color in a fraction of a second, yet most species have only one type of light receptor in their eyes, which should make them colorblind. Biologists have proposed that octopuses may detect color in another way: their unusual U-shaped pupils could separate light by wavelength, letting the animals sense color by how blurry different parts of an image appear. The hypothesis has not yet been confirmed experimentally.
choices: Octopuses are colorblind, which explains why their unusual pupils are shaped like the letter U.
Experiments have confirmed that the U-shaped pupils of octopuses separate light by its wavelength.
Biologists have proposed an unconfirmed explanation of how octopuses might perceive color.
Octopuses have more types of light receptors in their eyes than most other animals that change color.
r2009.explain: The text presents a puzzle (color change but one receptor type) and a proposed solution that "has not yet been confirmed." B contradicts that last sentence; D contradicts "only one type."

r2010.stem: Based on the text, what is the most likely reason Grandpa Ike pours a second cup of coffee each Sunday?
r2010.passage:
The following text is from a short story.

Every Sunday, Grandpa Ike set two cups on the porch table, filled both with coffee, and drank from one. When my cousin asked who the other cup was for, he said, "Whoever comes." In all the summers I visited, no one ever came, and every Sunday at noon he poured the second cup, cold and untouched, over the roses, which were the best on the street.
choices: He is expecting a particular friend who once promised to visit him on a Sunday.
He wants to show that he is ready to welcome any visitor, even though none arrives.
He uses the second cup of coffee to fertilize his roses, which are the best on the street.
He forgets each week that he has already poured a cup of coffee for himself.
r2010.explain: His answer, "Whoever comes," shows the cup is for no one in particular; it signals openness to a visitor. A contradicts "Whoever." The roses get the leftover coffee, but that's a consequence, not the reason he pours it (C).

r2011.sub: Detail that supports the main point
r2011.stem: According to the text, how did Petra's builders make it possible for a large population to live in a dry place?
r2011.passage: The ancient city of Petra, carved into sandstone cliffs in what is now Jordan, received only about 15 centimeters of rain a year. Yet it supported as many as 20,000 people. The Nabataeans who built it captured almost every drop: channels cut into the rock carried runoff from the surrounding hills to underground cisterns, and clay pipes delivered water throughout the city. Archaeologists estimate that the system could store millions of liters.
choices: They used clay pipes to import water from rivers in the hills surrounding the city.
They kept the city's population small enough that the limited rainfall could support it.
They chose a location in the hills where rain fell far more often than in the surrounding desert.
They built a system that collected rainwater and runoff and stored it for later use.
r2011.explain: The text describes channels carrying runoff to cisterns and pipes distributing the stored water. The pipes moved water within the city, not from distant rivers (A). C contradicts the low rainfall.

r2012.sub: Main idea of a reflective passage
r2012.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
r2012.passage:
The following text is from an essay by a translator.

People often ask which of my translations is most faithful, as if faithfulness were a single thing. But a sentence can be faithful to the original's meaning and unfaithful to its music, or faithful to its rhythm while losing a pun on which the whole paragraph turns. Every translation chooses among loyalties. The best I can do is choose deliberately, and know what I have given up.
choices: Translation means choosing among kinds of faithfulness, and the translator should choose knowingly.
A good translation preserves every feature of the original, including its meaning, rhythm, and wordplay.
Faithfulness to an original text's meaning is less important than faithfulness to its sound and rhythm.
Readers who care about faithfulness should avoid translations and learn to read works in the original.
r2012.explain: The writer argues that faithfulness has several forms that conflict ("Every translation chooses among loyalties") and that the translator should "choose deliberately." B is the view the essay rejects. C ranks one loyalty above another, which the writer never does.

r2013.sub: Main idea that reverses an assumption
r2013.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
r2013.passage: For years, physicians advised parents to keep peanuts away from infants to prevent peanut allergies. A large clinical trial changed that advice. Infants at high risk of allergy who were regularly fed small amounts of peanut protein starting before their first birthday were far less likely to develop a peanut allergy by age five than similar infants who avoided peanuts. Guidelines in many countries now recommend introducing peanut foods early for most infants.
choices: Infants at high risk of allergy should not be given peanut foods until after their fifth birthday.
A trial found that early exposure to peanuts lowers allergy risk, reversing earlier advice.
Peanut allergies that develop in early childhood usually disappear by the time children turn five.
Physicians have stopped testing infants for allergies because early exposure prevents them.
r2013.explain: The text contrasts old advice (avoid peanuts) with a trial showing early exposure reduced allergies, and notes that guidelines changed. A is the old advice the trial overturned. The trial measured who developed an allergy, not whether allergies disappear (C).

r2014.stem: Which choice best describes what Rafael realizes at the end of the text?
r2014.passage:
The following text is from a novel. Rafael, a young violinist, has just played for a famous teacher.

Rafael finished the sonata and waited for the verdict. The old man only asked him to play the opening again, slower. Then again, slower still, until the first phrase stretched so long that Rafael could hear, inside each note, the small unevenness of his bow that speed had always hidden. When the teacher finally nodded, Rafael understood that he had not been judged at all. He had been shown.
choices: The teacher was disappointed by his playing and had decided not to accept him as a student.
He should always play the opening of the sonata as slowly as possible when performing it.
The teacher had not listened carefully to his first performance of the sonata.
The teacher's requests were meant to show him a flaw rather than to judge him.
r2014.explain: Playing slower exposed "the small unevenness of his bow," and Rafael concludes he "had not been judged" but "shown." The slow playing was a teaching method, not a rule for performing (B). Nothing indicates disappointment (A).

r2015.stem: According to the text, what is the purpose of expansion joints?
r2015.passage: Most bridges expand in summer and contract in winter. To keep the structure from cracking, engineers include expansion joints: gaps, often bridged by interlocking metal teeth, that let sections of the deck slide slightly as their length changes. On a long steel bridge, the total movement across a joint can exceed half a meter between the hottest and coldest days of the year.
choices: To strengthen a bridge so that it can support heavy traffic in both summer and winter
To prevent the sections of a bridge from expanding on the hottest days of the year
To let parts of a bridge change length with temperature without cracking
To connect sections of a bridge made of steel to sections made of concrete
r2015.explain: Joints "let sections of the deck slide slightly as their length changes," which keeps the structure "from cracking." They allow expansion rather than prevent it (B). Traffic and mixed materials aren't mentioned.

r2034.passage: Plant physiologist Nadia Petrov grew two varieties of wheat under normal watering and under drought conditions and measured grain yield. She concluded that variety K is more drought tolerant than variety M: although K yields less than M when water is plentiful, it loses a smaller share of its yield when water is scarce.
choices: Under normal watering, variety M yielded 1.0 ton per hectare more than variety K, a difference of 20%.
Under drought, variety K's yield fell by 20% from its normal level, while variety M's yield fell by 40%.
Under drought, variety K yielded 4.0 tons per hectare, while variety M yielded 3.6 tons per hectare.
Both varieties yielded less under drought, and variety K yielded more than variety M under drought.
r2034.explain: The conclusion is about the share of yield lost. K: 5.05.0−4.0​=20%. M: 6.06.0−3.6​=40%. Only B compares the shares. A supports the first half of the sentence ("K yields less…"), not the conclusion. C gives one number with no comparison.

r2035.sub: Completing a claim with a trend
r2035.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?
r2035.passage: Ornithologists counted migrating hawks passing over a ridge each autumn. The graph shows the counts for two species. Counts of broad-winged hawks varied widely from year to year, but counts of red-tailed hawks
choices: fell steadily, declining from each year to the next from 2019 through 2024.
were lower than counts of broad-winged hawks in every year from 2019 through 2024.
were highest in 2019, when about 1,500 red-tailed hawks were counted.
never exceeded 2,000 in any year that the ornithologists counted.
r2035.explain: The sentence contrasts the wild swings of broad-winged hawks with red-tailed hawks, so the completion should describe a steady pattern: a decline every year. B, C, and D are all true, but none provides the contrast with "varied widely."

r2036.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the researcher's point?
r2036.passage: A city introduced a bike-share program in 2021. A local official claims that the program reduced car traffic downtown, citing a drop in the average number of cars entering downtown each weekday after 2021. A transportation researcher notes that the official's comparison leaves out a nearby city that did not introduce bike sharing.
choices: The city with bike share had more downtown car traffic than the nearby city in both years.
Car traffic in the city with bike share fell from 84,000 to 76,000 cars per weekday.
Car traffic fell by about 10% in both cities, even though only one introduced bike sharing.
In 2022, the nearby city had 63,000 cars entering downtown per weekday.
r2036.explain: The researcher's point is that the comparison needs a city without bike sharing. Traffic fell about 9.5% (84 to 76) in one city and 10% (70 to 63) in the other, so the drop happened without bike sharing too, which undercuts the official's causal claim. r2037.passage: Researchers surveyed visitors to three national parks about how they first heard about the park. The researchers claim that social media was a more important source of information for visitors to Park Y than for visitors to Park X.
choices: Social media was cited by 30% of Park Z visitors, more than any other source except friends or family.
Friends or family were cited by 41% of Park X visitors, more than any other source for that park.
Travel guides were cited by fewer Park Y visitors (18%) than Park X visitors (25%).
Social media was cited by 39% of Park Y visitors, the most of any source, but by just 22% of Park X visitors.
r2037.explain: The claim compares social media's importance for Park Y and Park X, so the evidence must give social media's figure for both parks: 39% versus 22% (and for Park Y it is the top source). A is about Park Z. B and C describe other sources, not social media.

r2038.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support the analyst's claim?
r2038.passage: An energy analyst tracked the share of a region's electricity generated from coal and from wind between 2016 and 2024. The analyst claims that by the end of the period, wind had overtaken coal as a source of electricity in the region.
choices: Coal's share of electricity fell in every year shown.
Wind's share of electricity rose from 9% in 2016 to 20% in 2020.
In 2024, wind generated 33% of the region's electricity, while coal generated 17%.
In 2016, coal generated more than five times as much of the region's electricity as wind did.
r2038.explain: "Overtaken by the end of the period" requires comparing the two sources at the end: in 2024, wind (33%) exceeds coal (17%). A and B each describe only one source, and D describes the beginning of the period.

r2039.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Aydin's claim?
r2039.passage: In a study of a new reading program, students were randomly assigned either to the program or to their school's usual lessons. Education researcher Kemal Aydin claims that the program helped struggling readers more than it helped strong readers.
choices: Struggling readers in the program gained 15 points, the most of any group in the study.
The program raised gains by 9 points for struggling readers but by only 3 points for strong readers.
Strong readers in the program gained 8 points, while strong readers in usual lessons gained 5 points.
Struggling readers gained more than strong readers in both the program and usual lessons.
r2039.explain: "Helped more" means a bigger improvement compared with usual lessons for each group: 15−6=9 versus 8−5=3. A ignores the baseline. D is true but shows only that struggling readers gain more in general, not that the program helped them more.

r2040.sub: Bar graph and a qualified claim
r2040.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support the researcher's claim?
r2040.passage: A sleep researcher measured how long it took participants to fall asleep after using a phone, reading a printed book, or doing neither during the hour before bed. She claims that reading a printed book did not delay sleep, while using a phone did.
choices: Participants took 26 minutes to fall asleep after using a phone, nearly twice as long as after doing neither.
Participants fell asleep fastest after doing neither, taking an average of only 14 minutes.
Participants took one minute longer to fall asleep after reading a printed book than after doing neither.
Sleep came about as fast after reading (15 minutes) as after doing neither (14), but took 26 minutes after phone use.
r2040.explain: The claim has two parts: reading did not delay sleep (compared with doing neither) and phones did. D gives the evidence for both. A covers only the phone, C only the book, and B mentions neither.

r2041.passage: A conservation group reported population counts for two endangered frog species at a wildlife refuge. The group claims that, relative to their starting populations, species B recovered more strongly than species A between 2015 and 2025.
choices: Species B's population increased by 150%, while species A's increased by 40%.
Species A's population increased by 160 frogs, while species B's increased by 120 frogs.
In 2025, there were more adult frogs of species A than of species B.
Both species had more adult frogs in 2025 than in 2015.

choices: Glacier R retreated farther in 2010–2020 (260 meters) than in 2000–2010 (210 meters).

Glacier S retreated 890 meters in 2000–2010 and 1,120 meters in 2010–2020.
both glaciers retreated faster in the second decade than in the first.

She recorded visits per hour to a meadow's flowers at different wind speeds. The data do not support her prediction for the highest wind speeds tested, however:
choices: visits were most frequent at wind speeds of 0–5 km/h.
visits fell from 48 per hour to 41 per hour as wind speed rose from 0–5 km/h to 6–10 km/h.
visits were slightly more frequent at 16–20 km/h than at 11–15 km/h.
there were fewer visits at 16–20 km/h than at 0–5 km/h.

r2044.passage: A museum offered free admission on Thursday evenings to attract visitors who rarely visit museums. The museum's director claims that the program succeeded: on free evenings, a larger share of visitors were first-time visitors than on regular days.
choices: The museum averaged 300 more visitors on free Thursday evenings than on regular weekdays.
The museum averaged 600 first-time visitors on free Thursday evenings, compared with 240 on regular weekdays.
Most visitors on free Thursday evenings were not first-time visitors.
First-time visitors made up 40% of visitors on free Thursday evenings but only 20% on regular weekdays.
r2044.explain: The claim is about the share of first-time visitors: 1,500600​=40% versus 1,200240​=20%. A compares total attendance. B compares counts, but total attendance also differed, so counts alone can't show a larger share. C is true but works against the director's emphasis.

r2045.sub: Scatter of data and a correlation claim
r2045.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the scatterplot to support the team's claim?
r2045.passage: A team of agronomists measured soil organic carbon and average crop yield on 10 farms. The team claims that farms with more soil organic carbon tended to have higher yields.
choices: Farms above 3% organic carbon yielded over 5 tons per hectare; farms below 1.5% yielded under 4 tons.
One farm had soil organic carbon of 2.5% and a yield of 4.2 tons per hectare, lower than a farm with 2.2%.
No farm had a yield greater than 6 tons per hectare, regardless of its level of soil organic carbon.
Soil organic carbon ranged from about 1% to about 4% across the 10 farms in the study.
r2045.explain: A "tended to" claim is supported by comparing high-carbon farms with low-carbon farms: the highest-carbon farms yield above 5 tons, the lowest below 4. B is a single point, and C and D describe ranges, not the relationship.

r2046.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the researcher's argument?
r2046.passage: A public health researcher compared two counties' rates of a disease. She argues that although County F reported more cases, the disease was actually more common in County G once population size is taken into account.
choices: County F had 640 more reported cases than County G in 2024, even though it is the larger county.

r2047.sub: Graph of change over time with a turning point
r2047.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support the historian's claim?
r2047.passage: A historian studying a nineteenth-century port city claims that the city's population grew rapidly after a railroad connected it to inland farms in 1850, after decades of little change.
choices: The population grew by about 3,000 from 1820 to 1850 but by about 39,000 from 1850 to 1870.
The population was about 63,000 in 1870, three times what it had been in 1820.
The population was larger in 1860 than in 1850, and it was larger still in 1870, two decades after the railroad.
The population was about 21,000 in 1820 and about 24,000 in 1850.
r2047.explain: The claim contrasts slow growth before 1850 with rapid growth after. A gives both: about 3,000 over thirty years, then about 39,000 over twenty. D covers only the years before 1850, C only the years after, and B merges the two periods into one overall change that hides the contrast.

r2049.passage: A city surveyed residents before and after it extended library hours into the evening. A council member claims that the change did not reduce daytime library use.
choices: After the extension, the library averaged 310 evening visits per day, up from none before the change.

r2050.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support the researchers' conclusion?
r2050.passage: Psychologists tested whether background music affects memory. Participants memorized word lists in silence, with instrumental music, or with music that had lyrics, and were tested immediately and again one week later. The researchers concluded that music with lyrics hurt long-term recall more than it hurt immediate recall.
choices: Participants who heard lyrics recalled 38% of words one week later, the lowest of any condition at either time.
Compared with silence, lyrics cut recall by 11 points on the immediate test but by 17 points a week later.

r2016.sub: Finding that would weaken a hypothesis
r2016.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Brandt's hypothesis?
r2016.passage: Many songbirds sing more loudly in cities than in forests. Biologist Ilse Brandt hypothesizes that the change is a direct response to traffic noise: birds raise their volume only when background noise is high, much as people raise their voices in a noisy room.
choices: City birds sing just as loudly on quiet Sunday mornings, when traffic is light, as during weekday rush hours.
City birds sing more loudly in parks next to highways than in parks far from any major road, even at the same time of day.
Forest birds that hear recordings of traffic noise played through speakers begin singing more loudly within a few days.
City birds sing at noticeably higher pitches than forest birds of the same species, which helps their songs carry over noise.
r2016.explain: Brandt says birds raise volume only when noise is high. If they sing just as loudly when traffic is light, the volume doesn't track noise, which weakens the hypothesis. B and C support it. D concerns pitch, not volume.

r2017.stem: Which quotation from the novel most effectively illustrates this claim?
r2017.passage: In the novel The Lantern Keeper, the narrator describes her aunt Maud as someone whose generosity is real but always comes with a reminder of what it cost her.
choices: "Maud kept her savings in a tin box under the floorboards and counted every coin of it each Friday night after supper."
"When the roof leaked that spring, Maud paid for all of the repairs herself, without telling any of us what it cost."
"Maud bought me a good wool coat that winter and mentioned at every meal that week how she would now go without boots."
"Maud was the first in the family to finish school, and she reminded us of it at every holiday dinner for twenty years."
r2017.explain: The claim has two parts: real generosity and a reminder of its cost. The coat is generous, and the repeated mention of going without boots is the reminder. B shows generosity without any reminder. D shows reminding, but about schooling, not generosity.

r2018.sub: Evidence that supports a causal claim
r2018.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Asante's claim?
r2018.passage: Coral reefs that bleach during marine heat waves sometimes recover. Marine ecologist Kofi Asante claims that reefs with abundant plant-eating fish recover faster, because the fish graze on algae that would otherwise smother young corals before they can grow.
choices: Plant-eating fish are more common on reefs in warm tropical waters than on reefs in cooler waters farther from the equator.
After a heat wave, reefs closed to fishing for plant-eating fish had fewer algae and more young corals than fished reefs.
Corals bleach when heat causes them to expel the tiny algae that live inside their tissues and supply most of their food.
Some coral species bleach at lower water temperatures than others, and those species tend to recover more slowly.
r2018.explain: The claim links plant-eating fish to faster recovery through algae grazing. Protected reefs with more of these fish having fewer algae and more young corals supports that chain directly. C is about the algae inside coral tissue, a different thing from the algae that smother young corals.

r2019.sub: Quotation that illustrates a poem's claim
r2019.stem: Which quotation from the poem most effectively illustrates this claim?
r2019.passage: In the poem "Harbor Town in Winter," the speaker suggests that the town, though quiet in winter, is still full of life.
choices: "The summer crowds are gone, their laughter gone, / the boardwalk bare beneath a pale gray sky"
"The gulls have taken the pier for their own / and quarrel there from morning until dark"
"I walked the empty beach from end to end / and met no one but wind and the long tide"
"The shutters closed, the boats pulled up and tarred, / yet every kitchen window burns till late"
r2019.explain: The claim has two parts: quiet and still alive. Closed shutters and boats pulled up show the quiet; windows lit late show life continuing. A and C show only emptiness. B shows gulls' activity, but not the town's life.

r2020.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the claim that water was poured to reduce friction?
r2020.passage: Some historians argue that ancient Egyptian builders moved the enormous stone blocks of the pyramids on wooden sledges dragged over sand, and that workers poured water in front of the sledges to reduce friction. A wall painting from a tomb shows a worker pouring liquid in front of a sledge carrying a statue.
choices: Other tomb paintings show workers carrying water jars at construction sites where large stone blocks were being moved.
Laboratory tests show that sand with the right amount of water roughly halves the force needed to drag a sledge across it.
Remains of wooden sledges strong enough to carry heavy stone blocks have been found buried near several of the pyramid sites.
Laboratory tests show that wetting sand increases, rather than decreases, the force needed to drag a heavy sledge across it.
r2020.explain: The explanation depends on water reducing friction. Tests showing that wetting sand makes dragging harder would undercut it. B would support the claim, and A and C are consistent with it.

r2021.stem: Which quotation from the memoir most effectively illustrates this claim?
r2021.passage: In her memoir, the scientist Lucinda Ford describes her relationship to her field notebooks as both practical and deeply personal.
choices: "My notebooks are waterproof and have numbered pages, so that none of my data can ever be lost, torn out, or altered."
"When I reread my old notebooks from graduate school, I sometimes find mistakes I made as a student and wince."
"I record the wind and time of every reading, and I've kept each notebook since I was nineteen, as others keep letters."
"I prefer a pencil to a pen in the field, because ink smears in the rain and pencil marks last for decades."
r2021.explain: Recording wind and time is practical; keeping every notebook "as others keep letters" is personal. A and D are only practical, and B doesn't show a personal attachment.

r2022.sub: Support for a generalization from a study
r2022.stem: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support Rahman's conclusion?
r2022.passage: Economist Ayesha Rahman studied a program that gave small grants to rural women in Bangladesh to start businesses. She concludes that the grants had lasting effects: women who received them were more likely to be running profitable businesses years after the program ended.
choices: Seven years later, recipients were twice as likely as similar women without grants to own a profitable business.
In the first month after the program began, most recipients used their grants to buy livestock or tools for a business.
Many recipients said in interviews years later that they still enjoyed running their own businesses and planned to continue.
The program gave grants to more women in its second year than in its first, and nearly all of them started businesses.
r2022.explain: "Lasting effects" requires evidence long after the program, and "profitable businesses" requires profit. A gives both, with a comparison group. B is too early to show lasting effects, and C shows enjoyment, not profitability.

r2023.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Castro's argument?
r2023.passage: A popular theory holds that the dinosaurs died out gradually over millions of years as volcanic eruptions slowly changed Earth's climate, and that the asteroid impact 66 million years ago merely finished off species that were already in steep decline. Paleontologist Rubén Castro disputes this, arguing that dinosaurs were thriving until the impact.
choices: Volcanic eruptions released large amounts of gas both before and after the asteroid struck Earth 66 million years ago.
Fossil records from the last million years before the impact show no decline in the number of dinosaur species.
The asteroid impact created a crater more than 150 kilometers wide and threw enormous amounts of debris into the atmosphere.
Some mammal species survived the asteroid impact and spread into many of the habitats that dinosaurs had occupied.
r2023.explain: Castro claims dinosaurs were thriving right up to the impact. Stable species counts in the final million years directly contradict the "steep decline" in the popular theory. A and C don't address whether dinosaurs were declining, and D is about mammals.

r2024.stem: Which quotation from the play most effectively illustrates this claim?
r2024.passage: In the play Second Harvest, the character Oren insists that he cares nothing for other people's opinions, but his actions suggest otherwise.
choices: OREN: "I have never asked anyone in this town for anything, and I never will." [He sits down heavily and folds his arms.]
OREN: "Let them talk. I need no one's approval." [He glances at the window to see whether the neighbors are watching.]
OREN: "The harvest will be late this year. Everyone knows it, and everyone is pretending not to worry."
OREN: "My father built this house with his own hands, and I will not sell it." [He runs a hand along the doorframe.]
r2024.explain: The claim pairs a stated indifference with behavior that contradicts it. In B, Oren says he needs no one's approval while checking whether the neighbors are watching. The actions in A and D fit his words rather than undercutting them, and C has no such contrast.

r2025.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly address the skeptic's concern?
r2025.passage: Students at a high school who took an optional course in personal finance had higher credit scores ten years later than students who did not take the course. A school board member argues that the course caused the higher scores. A skeptic replies that students who chose the course may already have had families who discussed money at home.
choices: Students who took the course reported years later that it was one of the most useful classes they took in high school.
The course covered budgeting, saving, and the use of credit cards, topics that are closely related to credit scores.
When a similar school made the course required, classes that took it later had higher credit scores than earlier classes.
Students who took the course were more likely than other students to attend college and to earn higher incomes afterward.
r2025.explain: The skeptic worries that students selected themselves into the course. Making the course required removes self-selection, so improved scores afterward point to the course itself. D could even support the skeptic, since college attendance may reflect family background.

r2026.sub: Quotation supporting a reading of a novel
r2026.stem: Which quotation from the novel most effectively illustrates this claim?
r2026.passage: In Elena Moreau's novel The Salt Road, the narrator's grandmother is presented as someone who expresses love through practical acts rather than words.
choices: "She never once said she was proud of me, but on the morning of my exam, new pencils lay sharpened on my desk."
"She told me every night, before she turned off the light, that I was the light of her life and her greatest joy."
"She was the most practical person I have ever known, and she had no patience for nonsense of any kind."
"She would sit by the window for hours in the evening, saying nothing at all, while I did my homework beside her."
r2026.explain: The claim has two parts: love shown through acts, not words. Never saying she was proud (no words) while leaving sharpened pencils (a practical act of care) fits both. B expresses love in words, and C describes practicality without love.

r2027.sub: Undermining an assumption in a proposal
r2027.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly undermine the council's assumption?
r2027.passage: A city council proposes planting thousands of trees in a low-income neighborhood to reduce summer heat, assuming that residents there lack shade because there is little space for trees along the streets.
choices: Neighborhoods with more street trees have lower summer temperatures, especially on the hottest afternoons.
Most residents of the neighborhood say in surveys that they support the council's tree-planting plan.
Newly planted trees take several years to grow large enough to provide significant shade for a street.
The neighborhood's streets have as many open planting spaces as streets in wealthier neighborhoods do.
r2027.explain: The assumption is that there's little space for trees. Abundant open planting spaces contradict it. A supports the plan's goal, not the assumption, and C raises a separate concern about timing.

r2028.sub: Support for an interpretation of an ancient object
r2028.stem: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support the researchers' argument?
r2028.passage: The Antikythera mechanism, a bronze device recovered from a shipwreck dated to about 70 BCE, contains dozens of interlocking gears. Researchers have long argued that it was a calculating device used to predict the positions of the Sun, the Moon, and possibly the planets.
choices: The same shipwreck also contained bronze statues and coins from several Greek cities, suggesting a wealthy cargo.
The device's gears were cut from a single sheet of bronze with remarkable precision for the period.
Inscriptions on the device name the planets and describe the cycles of lunar and solar eclipses.
Other shipwrecks from the same period have yielded scientific instruments such as simple sundials.
r2028.explain: Inscriptions naming planets and describing eclipse cycles tie the device's purpose to astronomical prediction. The other choices describe the setting or materials without bearing on what the device calculated.

r2029.sub: Which data would test a claim of preference
r2029.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Nwosu's claim?
r2029.passage: Some bumblebees are more likely to visit flowers with stripes than plain flowers of the same color. Entomologist Grace Nwosu claims that the bees are not born with this preference but learn it, because striped flowers in their region tend to hold more nectar.
choices: Bees in the region visit striped flowers more often than plain flowers of the same color and size.
Bees raised in a lab where plain flowers held more nectar than striped ones came to prefer plain flowers.
Striped flowers in the region hold more nectar, on average, than plain flowers of the same color.
Bees can see stripes in ultraviolet light that are invisible to humans, and many flowers have such stripes.
r2029.explain: To show the preference is learned, the evidence must show it changing with experience. Bees that learned to prefer plain flowers when plain flowers paid off show exactly that. A and C restate facts from the passage, which are consistent with either a learned or an inborn preference.

r2030.sub: Weakening a claim about a cause
r2030.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the company's claim?
r2030.passage: A study found that people who own dogs live longer, on average, than people who do not. A pet-food company claims in an advertisement that owning a dog increases life expectancy.
choices: People who are already healthy and physically active are more likely than others to choose to get a dog.
Dog owners walk more each day, on average, than people without dogs, and regular walking is linked to longer lives.
The study included thousands of participants from several countries and followed them for more than a decade.
Owning a cat is associated with a smaller increase in life expectancy than owning a dog.
r2030.explain: If healthier people are more likely to get dogs, their longer lives might reflect their health, not the dogs. B suggests a way dogs could help, which supports the claim. C strengthens the study's credibility.

r2031.stem: Which quotation from the poem most effectively illustrates this claim?
r2031.passage: In the poem "Field Notes," the speaker describes how her view of a marsh changes from boredom to fascination.
choices: "The marsh is wide and flat and smells of salt, / and the tide comes in twice daily, as it always has"
"I came because my mother asked me to, / and I stayed because the summer had nowhere else to go"
"By August, the heat had driven everyone indoors, / and the marsh was mine alone from dawn to dusk"
"At first I saw only reeds, and more reeds; / by August I could name the forty birds that hid in them."
r2031.explain: The claim describes a change from boredom to fascination. "Only reeds, and more reeds" conveys boredom, and learning the names of forty birds shows growing fascination. C marks time passing but shows no change in the speaker's view.

r2032.sub: Strengthening a claim with a natural experiment
r2032.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Oyelaran's claim?
r2032.passage: Linguist Marta Oyelaran claims that children learn new words faster when adults label objects the children are already looking at, rather than redirecting the children's attention to a new object.
choices: Children whose parents talk to them more often tend to have much larger vocabularies by the time they start kindergarten.
Toddlers pay more attention to brightly colored toys than to plain ones, and they hold the colored toys longer.
Older children learn new words faster than younger children do, whether or not adults label objects for them.
Toddlers whose parents named toys the toddlers were already holding learned more words than toddlers shown other toys.
r2032.explain: The claim compares labeling what the child is already attending to with redirecting attention. D tests exactly that comparison. A concerns the amount of talk, not its timing, and B and C are unrelated to labeling.

r2033.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Verbeek's argument?
r2033.passage: A painting long attributed to the seventeenth-century artist Judith Leyster was recently reexamined. Art historian Paul Verbeek argues that it is a nineteenth-century imitation rather than Leyster's work.
choices: The painting's subject, a young musician holding a lute, appears in several of Leyster's confirmed works from the 1630s.
The painting was owned by a single family for most of the twentieth century before it was sold at auction.
Chemical analysis shows that the painting contains a blue pigment that was not manufactured until the 1820s.
The painting's canvas is a type of linen commonly used by Dutch artists, including Leyster, in the 1600s.
r2033.explain: A pigment that didn't exist until the 1820s couldn't appear in a seventeenth-century painting, so the work must be later. A and D point toward the opposite conclusion, and B says nothing about when it was painted.

r2051.sub: Three facts that must all fit
r2051.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
r2051.passage: Archaeologists excavating a Bronze Age village in Scotland found bronze tools but no traces of copper or tin ore, the two metals needed to make bronze, within 200 kilometers of the site. They did find molds for casting tools and drips of solidified bronze on the workshop floor. Because bronze can be melted down and recast without losing quality, the archaeologists concluded that the village's metalworkers most likely
choices: mined small deposits of copper and tin near the village that the chemical analysis failed to detect.
imported all of their tools already cast and never worked bronze themselves.
obtained finished bronze objects through trade and recast them into new tools.
made most of their tools from a local metal and used imported bronze only for decoration.
r2051.explain: Three facts must fit together: no ore nearby, casting evidence on site, and bronze can be recast without losing quality. Only recasting traded bronze satisfies all three. A contradicts the absence of ore, B ignores the molds and drips, and D contradicts the bronze tools that were found.

r2052.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
r2052.passage: Ecologists noticed that a species of lizard on a small island had longer legs than the same species on the mainland. To test whether the difference was inherited or caused by the environment, they raised hatchlings from both populations in identical cages with identical food and perches. If the island lizards raised in captivity also developed longer legs than the mainland lizards raised in captivity, that result would suggest that
choices: the difference in leg length is at least partly inherited.
the difference in leg length is caused entirely by differences in the lizards' environments.
island lizards grow faster than mainland lizards in the wild.
longer legs make lizards better at climbing.
r2052.explain: Raising both groups in the same conditions removes environmental differences. If island lizards still grow longer legs, something other than the environment, likely heredity, is responsible. B reverses the logic of the control. C and D go beyond what the experiment tests.

r2053.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
r2053.passage: In 1906 an earthquake struck San Francisco. Official reports at the time listed about 375 deaths, but historians now estimate that more than 3,000 people died. The official count included few residents of Chinatown, whose deaths were often not recorded, and city leaders were eager to reassure investors that the city was safe to rebuild. These circumstances suggest that the official death toll was low because
choices: the earthquake itself was less destructive than historians now believe, since most deaths came later.
most residents of Chinatown had left the city in the weeks before the earthquake struck.
historians have overestimated the population of San Francisco in 1906 by relying on investors' reports.
many deaths in Chinatown went unrecorded and city leaders wanted to reassure investors.
r2053.explain: The text gives two circumstances: many deaths weren't recorded, and officials wanted to reassure investors. The completion must reflect both. A contradicts the historians' estimate; B and C are unsupported.

r2054.sub: An unexpected result in an experiment
r2054.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
r2054.passage: A biologist expected that adding nitrogen fertilizer to a grassland plot would increase the number of plant species growing there, since nitrogen is often scarce in grasslands. Instead, after five years, fertilized plots had fewer species than unfertilized plots, although total plant mass was higher. A few tall, fast-growing grasses dominated the fertilized plots and shaded the ground. This pattern suggests that
choices: nitrogen is not actually scarce in grasslands, so adding more of it had little effect on most species.
the fertilizer helped a few fast-growing species grow so large that they crowded out the others.
the fertilizer was toxic to most grassland plants, killing all but a few tolerant species.
the unfertilized plots produced more total plant mass because they supported a greater variety of species.
r2054.explain: More total mass but fewer species, with tall grasses shading the ground, points to competition: the fertilizer favored a few fast growers that crowded out others. C would not explain the higher plant mass, and D contradicts it. Nothing supports A.

r2055.sub: Conclusion from a pattern across sites
r2055.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
r2055.passage: Linguists studying a group of related languages in the Pacific found that the word for "sweet potato" is nearly identical across languages spoken on islands thousands of kilometers apart, and closely resembles the word used in Quechua, a language of South America, where the sweet potato was first domesticated. Since most researchers doubt that the plant could have crossed the ocean on its own, the linguistic evidence suggests that
choices: the sweet potato was first domesticated in the Pacific islands and later carried to South America.
Quechua is the ancestor of the Pacific languages, which explains the many words they share with it.
the Pacific languages borrowed the word from one another rather than from any language outside the region.
people carried the sweet potato, and its name, from South America to the Pacific islands.
r2055.explain: A shared word resembling the Quechua name, plus a plant unlikely to have crossed the ocean on its own, points to people carrying both the plant and its name. A contradicts the text. B overreaches from a single shared word to the ancestry of whole languages, and C contradicts the borrowing the text implies.

r2056.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
r2056.passage: A town's water utility found that household water use fell 12% after it installed new meters that let residents check their usage on a phone app. But the decline was the same in households that never downloaded the app as in households that used it daily. The new meters also replaced old ones that had been undercounting water use, and bills were based on the new readings. These findings suggest that the drop in water use was most likely caused by
choices: the app, which showed residents how much water they used and encouraged them to conserve it.
residents' responses to their higher and more accurate water bills rather than by the app itself.
a mistake in the new meters, which undercounted water use in households that never used the app.
households that used the app daily and shared conservation tips with neighbors who did not.
r2056.explain: The decline didn't depend on using the app, so the app isn't the cause (A). The new meters fixed undercounting, so bills likely went up, a reason everyone would cut back. C reverses which meters were inaccurate.

r2057.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
r2057.passage: A poem attributed to the medieval poet Aldric of Wensley survives in a single manuscript. The manuscript's paper contains a watermark that was used only between 1440 and 1460, and Aldric is known to have died in 1398. Since manuscripts are usually copies, the poem itself may be older than the paper. The watermark therefore shows only that
choices: Aldric could not have written the poem, since he died more than forty years before the paper was made.
the poem was composed between 1440 and 1460 by a writer who borrowed Aldric's name.
this particular copy of the poem was made no earlier than 1440, decades after Aldric's death.
Aldric wrote the poem shortly before his death and someone copied it immediately afterward.
r2057.explain: The watermark dates the paper, so this copy was made in 1440 or later. Because the text stresses that manuscripts are usually copies, the poem itself could be older, so A and B conclude too much. Nothing supports D.

r2058.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
r2058.passage: Students who eat breakfast tend to earn higher grades than students who skip it. To test whether breakfast itself improves performance, researchers provided free breakfast at school to a randomly chosen half of the students in a district. A year later, the grades of students offered breakfast had improved slightly more than those of other students, but the improvement was much smaller than the original grade gap between breakfast eaters and skippers. This result suggests that
choices: breakfast helps a little, but other differences between the groups likely explain most of the gap.
breakfast has no effect on students' grades, since the improvement was smaller than the original gap.
the original grade gap was caused entirely by breakfast, since grades improved when breakfast was provided.
students who skip breakfast would earn higher grades if their schools served lunch earlier in the day.
r2058.explain: The random assignment produced a small real effect, so breakfast matters somewhat, ruling out B. But the effect was much smaller than the original gap, so other factors must account for most of it, ruling out C.

r2059.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
r2059.passage: Some desert beetles collect drinking water from fog: tiny bumps on their backs attract water droplets, which then roll down grooves into the beetles' mouths. Engineers designing fog-harvesting nets have copied this structure. If the bumps work by attracting water while the surrounding surface repels it, then a net coated with a uniformly water-attracting material, with no repelling areas, would most likely
choices: collect less water, since droplets would spread into a film instead of gathering and rolling off.
collect more water, since every part of the net, not just the bumps, would draw droplets out of the fog.
collect water exactly as effectively as the beetles do, since it would copy their bumps precisely.
stop attracting water altogether, since the water-attracting material would repel the fog.
r2059.explain: The mechanism depends on contrast: attracting spots gather droplets and repelling surroundings let them roll away. Remove the repelling areas and water would spread into a film rather than gathering into droplets that roll down. B assumes more attraction is always better, which the mechanism contradicts.

r2060.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
r2060.passage: A seventeenth-century cookbook written in England gives measurements in cups and spoons rather than by weight, assumes readers know how to judge when an oven is hot by holding a hand inside it, and includes many recipes for preserving fruit but few for elaborate dishes requiring imported spices. These features suggest that the book was most likely written for
choices: readers who had never cooked before and needed simple measurements they could follow exactly.
professional cooks in wealthy homes who prepared fruit preserves for large households.
readers living outside England who could not obtain the imported spices used in English cooking.
experienced cooks in ordinary households rather than professional cooks in wealthy homes.
r2060.explain: Household measures and few imported spices point away from wealthy professional kitchens (B); assuming readers can judge oven heat by hand points away from beginners (A). Experienced household cooks fit all three features.

r2061.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
r2061.passage: Astronomers searched the light from 2,000 nearby stars for periodic dips that would indicate an orbiting planet passing in front of its star. A planet is detected this way only if its orbit is lined up edge-on as seen from Earth, which happens for only a small fraction of planetary systems. The astronomers found such dips for only 40 of the stars. Given these facts, it would be unreasonable to conclude that
choices: at least 40 of the 2,000 stars have one or more orbiting planets.
only 40 of the 2,000 stars that the astronomers studied have orbiting planets.
many of the 2,000 stars may have planets that this method could not detect.
planets whose orbits are not lined up edge-on cannot be found by this method.
r2061.explain: The question asks for the unreasonable conclusion. Because only edge-on orbits produce dips, many planets go undetected, so finding dips at 40 stars can't mean only 40 have planets. A, C, and D are all reasonable given the text.

r2062.sub: Combining a rule with an observation
r2062.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
r2062.passage: In many bird species, the sex of a chick that hatches first has an advantage, because it is larger than its later-hatching siblings. In one species of hawk, females are larger than males. Researchers found that hawk mothers in good years, when food was plentiful, tended to lay male eggs first, giving the smaller sex a head start. In poor years, they laid female eggs first. This suggests that in poor years, mothers
choices: lay more eggs than in good years so that at least some chicks survive the shortage of food.
are unable to control the order in which they lay male and female eggs when food is scarce.
may give the head start to the larger sex, whose bigger size helps it survive scarce years.
prefer to raise male chicks, since males need less food than females do in poor years.
